book.title: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team
book.author: Patrick Lencioni

confidence_note: TITLE-CONTENT MISMATCH (partial): the title asks why Lencioni read a team problem as a trust problem rather than a strategy problem. The book's model puts absence of trust at the base, and the fable follows the CEO of a fictional company; Lencioni's own consulting origin of the idea was not verified and is not used. Verified from catalog/summary sources: it is a leadership fable, the CEO is Kathryn Petersen of DecisionTech, the first dysfunction is absence of trust (unwillingness to be vulnerable within the group), the second is fear of conflict (artificial harmony over passionate debate). The names of the other three dysfunctions are from common knowledge of the model. Omitted: the company's location, offsite scenes, other characters, results of the fictional team.
facts: The book is a leadership fable, not a case study: its team is fictional.
The CEO in the fable is Kathryn Petersen of the company DecisionTech.
Lencioni's model names five dysfunctions in a pyramid: absence of trust, fear of conflict, lack of commitment, avoidance of accountability, inattention to results.
Trust sits at the base: it means team members are willing to be vulnerable with one another.
The second layer, fear of conflict, is a team choosing artificial harmony over passionate debate.

Each layer rests on the one under it, so the model says a team that cannot be open about mistakes and weaknesses will also avoid arguing, commit weakly, dodge accountability and lose focus on results.
The fable's setting makes the point that the trouble is in how the people deal with each other, not in a missing plan.
scene_details: a pyramid with trust at the bottom
a CEO, Kathryn Petersen, taking over at DecisionTech
a team choosing harmony over honest argument
tension: A team with every reason to succeed is stuck, and the book says the root is not in the plan but at the bottom of the pyramid.
opening_idea: Open on Kathryn Petersen taking over DecisionTech, a company whose problem is not its plan.

lessons.idea: When a team stalls, look first at whether people can admit mistakes and weaknesses to each other, because everything above that depends on it.
lessons.anchor: trust at the base of the five-layer pyramid

reflect_final: In the team you work with most, what is one mistake or doubt people usually keep to themselves, and who could say theirs aloud first?

use_cases.situation: A meeting where everyone nods and nothing moves.
use_cases.move: Say that in Lencioni's model, fake harmony sits just above missing trust, and ask each person to name one thing they would normally keep quiet.

use_cases.situation: One-on-one with someone who hides problems.
use_cases.move: Admit a recent mistake of your own first, then ask what they are unsure about.

use_cases.situation: A group of friends planning a trip stays vague.
use_cases.move: Ask each person to say one thing they do not want, before anyone proposes a plan.

pocket_idea: Lencioni's pyramid starts at trust: no plan holds if the people cannot admit mistakes to each other.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: In Lencioni's pyramid, the base of a team is not strategy but the willingness to admit mistakes in front of each other.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Lencioni told his team theory as a fable: Kathryn Petersen takes over DecisionTech. The five dysfunctions form a pyramid with trust at the bottom, meaning being willing to be vulnerable, then fear of conflict, and so on up to ignoring results. His point is that the base cracks first.
